newsitem.title: SOMALIA: American aid worker kidnapped in north Mogadishu.
newsitem.headline: American aid worker kidnapped in north Mogadishu.

text.p: Gunmen kidnapped an American working for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) in the northern part of Somalia's capital on Tuesday.

Witnesses said American Daniel Suther was seized by more than eight gunmen who intercepted his vehicle on Sanaa road in north Mogadishu and fired in the air shortly after he met a local faction leader.

The gunmen disarmed Suther's two Somali guards in his four-wheel-drive vehicle and drove off with him and his Somali driver towards the coastal town of Uarsciek, some 50 km (30 miles) northeast of the capital, security sources said.

They said Ali Mahdi Mohamed, whose Abgal clan alliance controls north Mogadishu, ordered an Islamic court to seize the kidnappers and also sent two "technicals", four-wheel-drive battlewagons, to Uarsciek to recover the American.
Suther was taken shortly after meeting Ali Mahdi, they said.
The U.S. embassy in Kenya's capital Nairobi confirmed an American working for USAID was kidnapped in north Mogadishu.

In Washington, USAID Spokeswoman Ann Kittlaus said the kidnapped man, whom she did not identify, was on contract with USAID and was a member of a three-person team sent to check on the food situation in north Mogadishu.
She said the other two members of the team were released but he was still being held. "Everyone to our knowledge is safe", including the kidnapped man, she added but gave no more details.

Kidnappings and extortion, especially involving staff of foreign aid agencies, are common in Mogadishu, where weapons are easily available and unemployment is extremely high since the departure of the U.N. peacekeeping operation in March 1995.
International aid agencies pulled all foreign staff out of southern Mogadishu, controlled by forces loyal to faction leader Hussein Aideed, earlier this year, but kept some staff in north Mogadishu.
The northern part of the city was widely considered far less dangerous than the south for foreigners under the control of Ali Mahdi's forces and gunmen who enforce Islamic sharia law.

Islamic courts have been increasing their scope in recent months and earlier this month ordered that foreign aid workers and journalists in north Mogadishu could not be escorted by their own armed guards as the sector of the capital was safe.
Ali Mahdi supported U.S. military intervention in Somalia in December 1992 in Operation Restore Hope to help end famine and the subsequent U.N. peacekeeping operation in 1993 and 1994.

Somali gunmen have abducted more than 20 aid workers in the last three years in disputes over money. All were freed unharmed after negotiations but several foreigners were killed in other incidents. Somalia has had no central government or authority since the overthrow of late dictator Mohamed Siad Barre in 1991.
